Meta.Title: Transparent Personal RAG Pipeline + MCP Server (ChatGPT, YouTube, Notes)

Section.name: High-Level Description
Section.IntroParagraph: Build a personal, transparent RAG pipeline (exposed “knobs”, end-to-end visibility, explainable retrieval) that ingests my official ChatGPT export history first, then YouTube transcripts (with chapter-level retrieval), then my markdown notes/tickets; the system must summarize and deduplicate repetitive content while preserving grounded citations back to original sources, and be usable daily via CLI, a Next.js UI, and an MCP server (query-only in v1).

SupportingBullets.Bullet: Primary persona: a single developer (learning-by-doing; prefers JavaScript/Node + Next.js, uses Python where it fits).
Core journey: ingest data sources → normalize + chunk → index → query via UI/CLI/MCP → inspect “why this was retrieved” → tune parameters → re-index.
Business value: reduce repeated conversations/debugging; faster recall of best practices and personal decisions; a durable personal knowledge base.
Out-of-scope (initially): multi-user SaaS, full auth/roles, enterprise-grade hosting, “one library does everything” opaque pipeline.
Constraints: local-first usage, ability to use local LLMs and OpenRouter, transparency/observability requirements, evolving schema/indexing strategy.

Goals.Goal: Within MVP, ingest official ChatGPT exports end-to-end (parse → normalize → chunk → summarize → dedupe/merge → embed → index) with deterministic re-runs.
Early v1 expansion: ingest YouTube transcripts with chapter metadata and support a “What’s new” / digest-like view grouped by chapter with tags.
Provide explainable retrieval: for every answer/query, show the retrieved chunks, scores/signals, and the pipeline decisions that produced them.
Provide a usable daily workflow via CLI and a Next.js UI, plus an MCP server query API for agent/tool integrations (Cursor/Cline-style usage).
Prefer after-the-fact inspection (trace log / waterfall) first, and only add real-time dashboards if needed.

NonGoals.NonGoal: Perfect “best possible” RAG quality at day 1; MVP optimizes for learning and transparency over raw quality.
Advanced access control, multi-tenancy, or syncing to a hosted cloud service.
Support for “any file type under the sun” in MVP (start with known formats and add iteratively).
MCP “write” / ingestion via MCP in v1 (query-only first; add later).

Row.UserStory: As a user, I want to ingest my official ChatGPT history exports into the system, so that past conversations are searchable and referenceable.

AcceptanceCriteria.Criterion: Given an official ChatGPT export (format documented by the project), when I run an ingest command, then the system parses, normalizes, and stores documents/chunks with stable IDs and source metadata.
Re-running ingest on unchanged inputs does not create duplicates (idempotent behavior).

EdgeCases.EdgeCase: Corrupted/partial export files are skipped with a clear error and do not break the whole ingest run.

Row.UserStory: As a user, I want the system to summarize and compress verbose conversations/notes into grounded summary chunks, so that the index is compact and less repetitive while still allowing me to trace back to original text.

AcceptanceCriteria.Criterion: Given an ingested document, when summarization runs, then it produces one or more summary chunks, each with citations back to the originating source ranges (message IDs / chunk IDs / timestamps).
Summaries are stored as first-class retrievable chunks and can be shown side-by-side with linked original sources.

EdgeCases.EdgeCase: If summarization fails for a document, the raw normalized chunks still ingest and the failure is visible/retryable.

Row.UserStory: As a user, I want deduplication/merge of highly-similar content (e.g., repetitive chats) to produce a “complete” merged chunk, so that near-duplicates don’t clutter retrieval while preserving unique details.

AcceptanceCriteria.Criterion: Given many near-duplicate summaries, when I query, then results can be grouped and clearly labeled as near-duplicates (retrieval-time grouping) with links to each original.

Optional: given two summary chunks with high overlap, the system can synthesize a merged representation that preserves unique details and links back to both originals (allowed at retrieval time first; ingest-time “master chunk” synthesis can be deferred if it adds too much complexity).

EdgeCases.EdgeCase: When overlap is borderline, the system can fall back to grouping (not merging) and surface this to the user.

Row.UserStory: As a user, I want to ingest YouTube transcripts with chapter-aware chunking, so that retrieval can return the most relevant chapter segment.

AcceptanceCriteria.Criterion: Given a transcript with chapters (or chapter timestamps), when ingested, then chunks include chapter metadata (title, start time, end time) where available.
When I query, the system can return chapter-scoped chunks and display that metadata in results.

EdgeCases.EdgeCase: Transcripts with no chapters still ingest with a fallback chunking strategy.

Row.UserStory: As a user, I want to ingest my local markdown notes/tickets/bug logs, so that recurring issues are searchable and reusable.

AcceptanceCriteria.Criterion: Given a folder of markdown files, when ingested, then documents are indexed with file path, modified time, and frontmatter tags (if present).
After parsing, the normalized content is stored and does not require referencing the original directory structure to query and retrieve.

EdgeCases.EdgeCase: Binary or unsupported files in the folder are ignored with a warning.

Row.UserStory: As a user, I want a transparent pipeline view of each stage (parse → normalize → chunk → summarize → dedupe/merge → embed → index), so that I can learn and tune each knob.

AcceptanceCriteria.Criterion: Given an ingest run, when I open the UI or run a CLI inspect command, then I can see per-stage configuration values and outputs (counts, timings, errors).
Given a single document, I can view its normalized text, derived chunks, summaries, and merged/deduped artifacts.
The UI provides a trace-log (“waterfall”) view per run, e.g., [Load] → [Normalize] → [Split] → [Summarize] → [Embed] → [Index], with timings and clickable artifacts.

EdgeCases.EdgeCase: If embedding fails for a subset of chunks, the failure is visible and retryable without redoing earlier stages.

Row.UserStory: As a user, I want explainable retrieval with grounding, so that I can see why a chunk was retrieved (and whether it was correct or duplicated) and always navigate back to the original source via citations.

AcceptanceCriteria.Criterion: Given a query, when results are returned, then the UI/CLI shows top-k chunks with their scores and contributing signals (e.g., vector similarity score, keyword match, recency boost).
Each result includes citations/links to original source locations (conversation/message IDs, file paths, transcript timestamps), and the system can display the cited original text.
For each query, the system logs the retrieval trace (inputs, configs, retrieved IDs) in a human-readable way.

EdgeCases.EdgeCase: If duplicate/nearly-duplicate chunks exist, the system can optionally de-duplicate or group them and show that grouping.

Row.UserStory: As a user, I want to query via a CLI, so that I can use the system quickly while working in the terminal.

AcceptanceCriteria.Criterion: CLI supports: ingest, re-index, query, inspect document/chunk, and export results.
CLI supports a config file and/or environment variables to change chunk sizes, embedding model, summarization/dedupe settings, and retriever settings.

EdgeCases.EdgeCase: If the server is not running, the CLI can still run offline operations (e.g., ingest/index) and warns for query operations that require a running service.

Row.UserStory: As a user, I want a Next.js UI (starting from an existing `flashbuild-llmcomparer` app) to visualize the pipeline, browse sources, and run queries, so that I can debug and tune the system.

AcceptanceCriteria.Criterion: UI supports: ingest status, corpus stats, config view, query view (results + explainability), and document/chunk browser.
UI highlights chapter metadata for YouTube content and conversation metadata for chat history.
From any result or trace step, I can click into a stored chunk/summary and immediately see its source citation(s); optionally show raw vector values behind an “advanced” toggle.

EdgeCases.EdgeCase: Large corpora do not freeze the UI; paging and server-side queries are used.

Row.UserStory: As a user, I want an MCP server interface (query-only in v1), so that my coding agents/tools can query and retrieve context from the same index.

AcceptanceCriteria.Criterion: MCP server exposes tools/endpoints for query and retrieval with citations to sources/chunks.
MCP server supports returning retrieval traces (optional) for debugging.

EdgeCases.EdgeCase: If MCP is disabled, core CLI/UI still works.

Row.UserStory: As a user, I want to choose which LLM/provider is used for each stage (summarization, dedupe assist, embeddings, synthesis), so that I can experiment with local models and OpenRouter.

AcceptanceCriteria.Criterion: Config supports selecting local models and OpenRouter-backed models per stage, with clear defaults.
The system records which model was used for each run and includes it in trace logs.

EdgeCases.EdgeCase: If a configured model is unavailable, the system fails fast with a clear error and suggested fallback.

Row.UserStory: As a user, I want a containerized/dev-friendly setup, so that I can run the pipeline reliably and reproduce the environment.

AcceptanceCriteria.Criterion: Provide a Docker-based setup (or equivalent) that can run the indexer and the UI/server components.
All configs are manageable via .env and checked-in sample configs (no secrets committed).

EdgeCases.EdgeCase: When running without Docker, local dev instructions still work.

Row.UserStory: As a user, I want a “What’s new” digest view for YouTube content (chapter-aware), so that I can browse recent material like a homepage/news feed and filter/sort by tags.

AcceptanceCriteria.Criterion: Given newly ingested YouTube transcripts, when I open the digest view, then I see a list grouped by video and chapter with the ability to sort/filter by tags and recency.
Each digest item includes citations/links back to the original transcript segment (and ideally the original video timestamp).

EdgeCases.EdgeCase: When chapters are missing, the UI shows a fallback grouping (e.g., semantic/temporal segments).

Row.UserStory: As a user, I want hierarchical chunking (chapter → semantic sub-chunks with overlap), so that I can retrieve precise details while keeping chapter context as a parent.

AcceptanceCriteria.Criterion: Given a transcript with chapters, when ingested, then chapters are stored as parent units and semantic overlapping sub-chunks are stored as children referencing the parent.
The UI can visualize the parent/child relationship as a “knob” (toggle retrieval on parent vs child; show how retrieval maps back to the parent chapter).

EdgeCases.EdgeCase: If chapter boundaries are missing, the system falls back to time-based or semantic segment parents.

UserFlow.Name: Initial setup and first ingest
UserFlow.Goal: Get first working index from at least one source

Steps.Step: User configures paths and models via .env/config.
System parses, normalizes, chunks, summarizes, groups near-duplicates (and optionally merges), embeds, and indexes; shows per-stage progress.
User runs a first query; views results and retrieval trace.

UserFlow.Name: Daily query + tuning loop
UserFlow.Goal: Retrieve useful context and tune pipeline knobs based on outcomes

Steps.Step: User enters a query (e.g., “how did I fix X bug last time?”).
System retrieves top-k chunks and shows explainability (scores, signals, metadata).
User marks results as good/bad (optional) and adjusts knobs (chunking, filters, dedupe, ranking weights).
User re-runs query and compares results and traces.

UserFlow.Name: YouTube “What’s new” digest
UserFlow.Goal: Browse new YouTube content by chapter and quickly open grounded sources

Steps.Step: System shows recent videos with chapter entries and extracted tags.
User filters/sorts by tags (positive/negative later) and opens a chapter item.
System shows the chapter summary plus citations to original transcript segments.

Component.Name: Ingestion + Normalization
Component.Option: Node.js-first ingestion pipeline with per-source adapters; Python subprocesses allowed for specialized parsing.
Python-first ingestion pipeline with a Node/Next UI wrapper.
Component.Tradeoffs: OptionA matches preference (“TypeScript-first”); OptionB may have stronger ecosystem for certain parsing/ML libs.

Component.Name: Storage / Index
Component.Option: LanceDB (embedded, file-based) with TypeScript SDK + metadata filtering for tags/facets.
ChromaDB as a local service (good for learning; more “explicit” operations).
Qdrant as a local service (more production-like server; more ops).
Component.Tradeoffs: OptionA best aligns with “inspect the data files” + TypeScript-first; Options B/C may be easier to follow tutorials or scale features but add a service boundary and operational complexity.

Component.Name: Retrieval + Ranking
Component.Option: Hybrid retrieval (vector + keyword + metadata filters) with configurable weighting and dedupe.
Component.Tradeoffs: Hybrid improves relevance and explainability but adds tuning surface area.

Component.Name: Interfaces
Component.Option: CLI + Next.js UI + MCP server sharing one backend.
Only CLI in MVP; UI/MCP later.
Component.Tradeoffs: OptionA fits stated goals; OptionB reduces MVP scope.

Component.Name: Repo / Packaging
Component.Option: Monorepo with separate packages: `pipeline` (core), `ui` (Next.js), `mcp-server` (query-only; calls pipeline).
Single package with all concerns co-located initially.
Component.Tradeoffs: OptionA clean boundaries for MCP + reuse; OptionB faster bootstrap but can get tangled.

Component.Name: LLM/Embedding Providers
Component.Option: Local LLMs (e.g., Qwen 8B/14B) for synthesis + local embeddings (TBD).
OpenRouter (free tier OSS where possible) for synthesis and/or embeddings.
Component.Tradeoffs: Use a combination: local-first where possible, OpenRouter for experimentation/comparison across pipeline stages.

Metric.Name: Ingest success rate
Metric.Definition: Number of successfully ingested documents/chunks divided by attempted documents/chunks per run.
Metric.SuccessThreshold: >= 99% for known-good inputs; failures are visible and actionable.

Metric.Name: Query usefulness (manual)
Metric.Definition: User-marked “useful” retrieval results divided by total queries (or per-query top-k usefulness).
Metric.SuccessThreshold: Initial target: >= 60% useful top-5 results for core workflows (bug recall, best-practice recall).

Metric.Name: Retrieval trace completeness
Metric.Definition: Percentage of queries where trace includes config, retrieved IDs, scores, and source metadata.

Metric.Name: Index rebuild time
Metric.Definition: Wall-clock duration to rebuild embeddings + vector index for the corpus.
Metric.SuccessThreshold: TBD (set after first baseline on target machine); must be observable and optimizable.

Risks.Risk: Transcript mentions a strong desire for transparency; picking “black box” libraries could undermine the learning goal.
ChatGPT export formats can change; ingestion adapters may need maintenance.
Embedding/model choice and chunking strategy could dominate quality; tuning surface area may cause scope creep.
Copyright/privacy concerns for storing and indexing third-party transcript content.
Summarization + dedupe/merge is a core requirement; if done poorly it can lose nuance or break grounding/citations.

Dependencies.Dependency: Access to ChatGPT export data in a known format.
A consistent method to obtain YouTube transcripts + chapters (source/format TBD).
Local model runtime availability (for Qwen 8B/14B) and/or OpenRouter credentials.
Starting codebase: copy/extend `/home/broz/playground/flashbuild-llmcomparer` to become the UI hub for pipeline stage experimentation.

OpenQuestions.Question: Decision: ChatGPT exports are official exports (confirm exact file layout of your existing export sets to lock parser assumptions).
How will YouTube transcripts be sourced (manual paste, API, yt-dlp, existing transcript files), and do you require chapter extraction?
Decision: LanceDB is the initial vector store (confirm whether we also want SQLite for additional relational metadata, or keep all metadata in LanceDB first).
Should v1 focus on retrieval + citations + trace only, or include answer synthesis (noting that summarization is required at ingest regardless)?
What metadata facets/tags matter most on day 1 (source type, author/channel, topic, project, recency, “importance”)?
What’s the minimum “pipeline visualization” you consider acceptable: after-the-fact inspection first (recommended), or real-time dashboard from day 1?
YouTube chunking strategy: chapter-only chunks vs chapter + overlapping semantic sub-chunks (recommended: both, with chapters as primary grouping and semantic chunks as retrievable units).
Deduplication strategy for v1: is retrieval-time grouping sufficient for MVP, with ingest-time “master chunk” synthesis deferred to later milestones?
